13130: "Quarry" has two main, completely unrelated meanings. They are so different that knowing both will prepare you to understand this word in any situation you ever encounter it.
Meaning 1 — A place where rock or stone is extracted from the earth

A quarry is a large, open-air excavation site — essentially a giant pit or cut into the earth — where workers extract stone, rock, or minerals for use in construction and other industries. Unlike an underground mine, a quarry is open to the sky. You can think of it as peeling layers of the earth back from above, rather than tunneling into it from below.

In a quarry, workers use heavy machinery, drills, and sometimes controlled explosives to cut or blast enormous quantities of rock from the earth's surface or from the steep walls of the pit. The rock extracted might be granite, limestone, marble, sandstone, slate, or gravel, depending on what naturally exists at that location. This material is then shaped, crushed, or processed and sent off to be used as building material — for roads, bridges, walls, monuments, floor tiles, and much more.

A quarry is typically a massive industrial site. Its walls are often cut in wide, descending terraces, like a giant staircase going down into the earth, which allows workers and machines to safely access the rock at each level. Over years and decades of operation, a quarry can grow to cover enormous areas and reach tremendous depths. When a quarry is no longer in use, the pit sometimes fills naturally with rainwater or groundwater, forming a quarry lake.

To put it in a sentence: "The ancient Romans sourced the travertine stone for the Colosseum from a quarry near Tivoli." Or: "She drove past the old abandoned quarry, its deep pit now a still lake surrounded by wildflowers."
Meaning 2 — The animal or person being hunted or chased

This meaning has nothing to do with stone or mining. Here, "quarry" refers to the target of a pursuit — the prey, the one being hunted.

The word in this sense originated in the world of hunting. When hunters and their hounds set out to chase a deer, a fox, or a bird, that animal — the one being chased — was called the quarry. The hunters themselves were never the quarry. The quarry is always the pursued, never the pursuer. This distinction is absolute.

Over time, the meaning broadened well beyond literal hunting and is now used in any context involving pursuit, tracking, or chasing. If a detective is tailing a suspect through city streets, the suspect is the detective's quarry. If a lion is chasing a zebra across a savanna, the zebra is the lion's quarry. If a spy is following a target across three countries, that target is the spy's quarry. The word can apply to humans or animals, real-world situations or fictional ones, and it carries a sense of intensity and focus — the quarry is not just someone wandering past; they are the specific, deliberate object of someone's chase or search.

This meaning often appears in literary, journalistic, and dramatic writing because it adds a vivid, almost cinematic quality. Saying "the detective cornered his quarry" feels far more alive and tense than simply saying "the detective caught the person he was chasing."

To put it in sentences: "The fox — the hunters' quarry — vanished into the undergrowth before the hounds could reach it." Or: "After a three-day manhunt, the fugitive, seemingly aware he had become the quarry, changed his appearance and abandoned his car."

One important nuance: because "quarry" implies an active, deliberate pursuit, it is rarely used for a passive or accidental encounter. The pursuer has chosen this specific target and is actively hunting them down.
Meaning 3 — A small pane of glass or a shaped tile (rare)

There is a third meaning that is much rarer and more specialized. In architecture, "quarry" can refer to a small, square or diamond-shaped pane of glass used in traditional latticed or leaded windows — the kind you might see in old English cottages or medieval churches. The word can also describe a floor tile of a similar shape. You are very unlikely to encounter this meaning in everyday reading, but if you ever see "quarry" used in the context of old windows or stonework and neither of the first two meanings fits, this is what it refers to.
How to tell which meaning applies

Since the three meanings are completely unrelated, context will almost always make it instantly obvious. If the sentence involves stone, rock, mining, construction, or a physical site — it is the pit in the earth. If the sentence involves chasing, hunting, tracking, fleeing, or pursuit — it is the prey or target. If it involves old windows or decorative tiles — it is the rare third meaning.

The only word that sounds like "quarry" is "query" (meaning a question), so be careful not to confuse the two in speech or reading.

What makes "quarry" an interesting word is precisely the fact that its two main meanings seem to have no logical connection — a stone pit and a hunted animal feel like they should be two different words entirely. Yet both are "quarry." This is simply the nature of how words evolve over centuries, absorbing different meanings from different sources along the way. What unites the word today is not a shared concept, but shared spelling and sound — and that is perfectly normal in English. The only job you have is to recognise which meaning applies from context, and as shown above, that is never really in doubt.
13131: A quarterback is the most important player on a team in American football. Think of them as the captain on the field — the person who touches the ball on almost every single play and decides what the team does next. If a football team were an army, the quarterback would be the commanding officer giving orders in real time.

To understand the word, you first need a tiny bit of context about American football. In this sport, one team tries to move an oval-shaped ball forward across the field and into the opponent's end zone to score points. The team that has the ball and is trying to score is called the offense, and the quarterback is the leader of the offense.

Here is what a quarterback does on every single play:

1. Receives the ball first.
At the start of each play, another player (called the center) hands or snaps the ball directly to the quarterback. This means the quarterback is the first one to touch the ball every time the offense begins a new move.

2. Makes an instant decision.
Within just a few seconds — sometimes less — the quarterback must decide what to do with the ball:

  • Pass (throw) it through the air to a teammate running downfield.
  • Hand it off to a nearby teammate who then runs forward with it.
  • Run with it themselves, if no better option is available.

3. Calls and communicates the plays.
Before each play begins, the quarterback tells their teammates exactly what everyone is going to do. They receive instructions from the coach (often through a speaker inside their helmet) and then relay the plan to the rest of the team. They can even change the plan at the very last second if they see something unexpected — this is called an audible.

4. Reads the opponent.
A great quarterback is always studying the opposing team while standing at the line. They're trying to predict where the defenders will move so they can make the smartest decision possible once the play starts.
Why the Quarterback Is So Special

In most team sports, no single player dominates the game quite the way a quarterback does in American football. Here's why they stand out:

  • They touch the ball on virtually every offensive play. A running back or a receiver might touch the ball a handful of times per game. The quarterback touches it dozens of times.
  • Every offensive play passes through them. Nothing happens on offense without the quarterback's hands and decision-making involved.
  • They are the face of the team. In American culture, when people talk about a football team, they almost always lead with the quarterback. Quarterbacks are typically the most famous, highest-paid, and most analyzed players in the sport.
  • They operate under enormous pressure. After receiving the ball, large opposing players rush toward them at full speed trying to tackle them before they can throw or hand it off. The quarterback must stay calm and make correct split-second decisions while this is happening.
Key Things to Know About the Position

• The pocket: When the quarterback drops back to throw, their own teammates form a protective wall around them. This protected space is called "the pocket." A quarterback who stays calm inside the pocket and makes good throws is called a pocket passer.
  • A scrambler or dual-threat quarterback: Some quarterbacks are also fast runners. Instead of always staying in the pocket, they run around, avoid tacklers, and gain yards themselves. These quarterbacks are called scramblers or dual-threat quarterbacks (meaning they can both pass and run effectively).
  • The most analyzed position in the sport: Quarterbacks are judged by statistics like how many passes they completed, how many touchdowns (scores) they threw, and how many times they threw the ball to the wrong team (called an interception).

When people hear "quarterback," names like Patrick Mahomes, Tom Brady, Joe Montana, and Peyton Manning come to mind — players considered legends of the sport, largely because the quarterback position is seen as the single most important role in the game.

Outside of football, quarterback is also used as a noun in everyday English to describe any person who leads, directs, or coordinates a complex effort — even if sports are not involved at all.

For example:

  • "She was the quarterback of the entire rescue operation."
  • "We need a strong quarterback to manage this project."

In these cases, the word simply means: the central, directing figure who keeps everything moving and makes the key calls. This usage borrows the football idea of someone who coordinates all the moving parts of a team.

A quarterback is the lead player of an American football team's offense — the one who receives the ball first on every play, decides what to do with it, and directs the entire team's attacking strategy — and, by extension, any person who serves as the central coordinator and decision-maker of a group effort.
13132: A quartermaster is a person in a military or naval organization whose job is to manage and provide essential support — though exactly what that support looks like depends on whether you're talking about an army (land forces) or a navy (sea forces). The word carries two distinct meanings in those two settings.

In an army, a quartermaster is the officer or soldier responsible for logistics — a word that simply means making sure troops get everything they need to survive and fight. This includes food, water, clothing, uniforms, weapons, ammunition, fuel for vehicles, medical supplies, and all equipment and gear.

Think of it this way: imagine an army of 10,000 soldiers is advancing across a desert. Who makes sure they have enough food, clean water, bullets, and fuel? That's the quartermaster. Without this person doing their job correctly, the army would fall apart long before it ever reached the enemy. Soldiers cannot fight on empty stomachs with no ammunition.

The quartermaster does not fight on the front lines. Their "battlefield" is the supply chain — warehouses, transport routes, vehicles, and inventories. Their job is to make sure the right things reach the right people at the right time.

In very large armies, this role can be held by an extremely senior officer called the Quartermaster General, who oversees the entire supply operation for the whole armed force.

In a navy, "quartermaster" means something noticeably different. Here, a quartermaster is a navigation specialist — a sailor whose job is to help steer and guide the ship safely. Their responsibilities typically include:

  • Maintaining nautical charts (maps of the sea and its routes)
  • Keeping the ship's log (the official written record of the voyage)
  • Assisting the officer on watch with navigation decisions
  • Sometimes physically taking the helm and steering the ship
  • Handling signals and communications in some navies

So the naval quartermaster is not about supplies at all — they are about making sure the ship goes where it's supposed to go, safely and accurately.
Why Does One Word Have Two Different Meanings?

It can seem confusing, but both meanings share a common thread: the quartermaster is a critical support role that keeps the larger operation running smoothly. In the army, they keep troops supplied. In the navy, they keep the ship on course. Neither fights on the front line, but both are absolutely indispensable to the mission.

The word is also used more loosely outside formal military settings. Any organization that deals with equipment and gear might call the person managing those supplies a quartermaster. For example, a sports team, a scout troop, or an expedition group might use the term informally for whoever is in charge of equipment.

In popular culture — especially in spy films, military fiction, and video games — you'll encounter the word often. The most famous example is the character "Q" in the James Bond films. His name is short for Quartermaster, and his role is precisely that: he equips James Bond with gadgets, weapons, and special tools before each mission. This is a direct use of the army meaning — he is the supply officer.

• "The quartermaster ensured that every battalion had enough rations before the long march."
  • "The ship's quartermaster carefully studied the charts as they entered the narrow strait."
  • "In the Bond films, Q is the quartermaster — the man who arms 007 with the tools he needs."
  • "The regiment's quartermaster was praised for keeping supply lines open despite the harsh weather."
The One-Line Summary to Remember Forever

• Army / general military context → Quartermaster = Supply officer (manages food, weapons, equipment, and all resources troops need).
  • Naval context → Quartermaster = Navigation specialist (manages charts, ship's log, and steering).

In both cases, the quartermaster is the person working behind the scenes to make the mission possible — the unsung backbone of any military operation.
13133: "Quarters" is the plural form of the noun "quarter." Since "quarter" itself carries several distinct meanings, "quarters" inherits all of them — and also has a few meanings that belong almost exclusively to its plural form.

A quarter is one part out of four equal parts. So quarters means multiple such parts, or all four parts together.

Think of an apple cut into four equal pieces. Each piece is a quarter. All four pieces together are the four quarters of the apple.

This idea extends everywhere:

  • A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes (since 60 ÷ 4 = 15). So "three quarters of an hour" means 45 minutes.
  • A quarter of a year is 3 months. Companies often divide their financial year into four such periods — called quarters (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4). You'll hear phrases like "our sales improved in the last two quarters."
  • A sports match (like basketball or American football) is divided into four periods of play. Each period is called a quarter. So people say things like "they dominated in the final two quarters."

A quarter is a coin used in the United States and Canada worth 25 cents — which is one-fourth of a dollar (since 100 ÷ 4 = 25). The plural, quarters, simply means more than one such coin.

"Do you have any quarters? I need them for the parking meter."
"She emptied her bag and found three quarters and a dime."

This meaning is specific to North American English.
Quarters as a Place to Live

This is one of the most important and distinctly plural uses of the word. Quarters (almost always in the plural) can mean a place where someone lives or sleeps, especially when that place is provided as part of a job or role.

The most common contexts:

  • Military quarters: Soldiers and officers are often provided housing on a base or in a barracks. This housing is called their quarters. An officer's home on a military base is called officer's quarters.

    "The soldiers returned to their quarters after the training exercise."

  • Servants' quarters: In large old houses or estates, the rooms where servants lived were called the servants' quarters — usually a separate section of the house.
  • Crew quarters: On a ship, the area where crew members sleep and rest is called the crew's quarters.

The key thing to understand here is that quarters in this sense means a designated living space — not necessarily luxurious, and often shared. You're not building it or buying it; it's assigned to you.

When people or things are at close quarters, they are very near to each other — sometimes uncomfortably so.

"The two fighters were battling at close quarters."
"Living in close quarters with strangers can be difficult."

The phrase "close quarters" originally came from naval warfare, where ships would sail so near each other that soldiers had to fight hand-to-hand. Over time it came to describe any situation of tight physical proximity. Today you can use it for people living in a small space, enemies fighting face-to-face, or even animals crowded together.
From All Quarters / From Every Quarter

Here, quarters is used to mean directions, sides, or sources. This is a somewhat formal or literary usage.

"Criticism came from all quarters." — meaning: criticism came from every direction, every group, every side.
"Help arrived from unexpected quarters." — meaning: help came from unexpected sources or people.

Think of the four directions on a compass — North, South, East, West. "All quarters" evokes this idea of completeness: every direction, every possible source.

In certain contexts, quarter (and by extension quarters) can refer to a distinct section or neighborhood of a city, especially one associated with a particular group of people or activity.

"They strolled through the old Arab quarter of the city."
"The artists' quarter was full of galleries and studios."

The most famous example is the French Quarter in New Orleans — a historic neighborhood with French and Spanish architectural influence. In this usage, the singular "quarter" is more common, but you may encounter "quarters" when referring to multiple such districts.

This is a phrase you'll encounter in historical, literary, or dramatic contexts. Quarter here means mercy shown to a defeated enemy — specifically, the decision to spare the life of someone who has surrendered.

  • "To give quarter" means to spare the lives of those who have surrendered.
  • "To show no quarter" or "to give no quarter" means to show absolutely no mercy — to fight to the death and refuse to spare anyone.

"The army was under orders to give no quarter."
"The cornered soldiers asked for quarter, but the general refused."

The origin lies in old battlefield practice, but today this expression appears in both literal (war) and figurative (competition, conflict) contexts:

"In the final debate, she gave no quarter to her opponents." — meaning she attacked relentlessly and showed no leniency.

Hindquarters is a compound word, but you'll often hear just "quarters" used in the context of animals to refer to their rear section — the back half of a large animal's body, including the hips and back legs.

"The horse's quarters were powerfully muscled."
"A quarter of beef" refers to one of the four large sections a cow's carcass is divided into for butchering.

Here is a quick mental map of everything "quarters" can mean:

  • Fractions: Four equal parts of something (an apple, an hour, a year, a game).
  • Coins: 25-cent coins in the US/Canada.
  • Living space: A place to sleep/live, especially assigned housing in the military or on a ship.
  • Close quarters: Very close physical distance.
  • All quarters: All directions or all sources.
  • City district: A neighborhood defined by culture or character.
  • No quarter: No mercy in a fight or competition.
  • Animal anatomy: The rear portion of an animal's body.

The thread connecting almost all of these is the idea of division and allocation — whether it's dividing something into four equal parts, dividing a city into sections, dividing a year into periods, or allocating someone a place to live.
13134:
A quarto is a type of book (or a single document) made by taking a large, full sheet of paper and folding it twice — first in half, and then in half again. This double-folding produces four separate leaves (which gives you eight pages, since every leaf has a front and a back). Each of those leaves is exactly one-quarter the size of the original full sheet.

That is the heart of the word. A quarto is not just a size — it is a format, meaning it describes how the book was made, specifically how the paper was folded during its production.

Think of it like this. Take a large, flat sheet of paper — like a big newspaper page.

  • Fold it once and you get two leaves (four pages). That format is called a folio.
  • Fold it twice and you get four leaves (eight pages). That format is a quarto.
  • Fold it three times and you get eight leaves (sixteen pages). That is an octavo.

A quarto sits in the middle of this family. It is smaller than a folio but larger than an octavo. Because the sheet has been folded twice, the pages of a quarto are a quarter of the original sheet in size — which is where the name comes from (it means "fourth" or "quarter").
What Does a Quarto Actually Look Like?

In terms of physical size, a quarto is roughly what we today might call a "large book" — typically somewhere around 9 to 12 inches tall and 7 to 9 inches wide, though the exact measurements varied depending on the size of the original printing sheet used by different printers in different eras. Quartos were notably taller than they were wide, giving them a somewhat upright, rectangular shape.

To put it in everyday terms: a quarto is roughly the size of a modern A4 or letter-sized piece of paper. If you imagine a standard sheet of printer paper as a book, you have a rough mental picture.
Why It Matters: The World of Early Printing

The concept of a quarto is most important in the context of historical books and manuscripts, especially from the era of early printing (the 1400s through the 1700s). Back then, printers didn't have pre-cut paper in fixed sizes the way we do today. They worked with large master sheets and folded them in different ways to produce books of different sizes. The number of times they folded the sheet — and the way they arranged the text on the master sheet before folding — determined the final format of the book.

The quarto format was extremely popular because it struck a practical balance: it was smaller and cheaper than a folio (making it more affordable and portable), but still large enough to print clearly and hold a substantial amount of text.
The Shakespeare Quartos — The Most Famous Example

When people talk about quartos in literature, the most well-known examples are the Shakespeare quartos. Many of William Shakespeare's plays were first published during his lifetime (late 1500s to early 1600s) as individual quarto pamphlets — thin, small booklets sold cheaply to the public, each containing a single play. These were not grand, collected editions; they were affordable, compact publications, much like a modern paperback.

Scholars and historians refer to these as "the quartos" of Shakespeare's works, and they are studied intensely because they sometimes differ from the more authoritative text collected after Shakespeare's death in the famous First Folio of 1623. Some quartos are considered reliable ("good quartos"), while others are thought to be reconstructed from memory or otherwise imperfect ("bad quartos").

Today, the word "quarto" is used in two main contexts:

1. In bibliography and book history: This is where the term is most precisely used. Scholars, librarians, and book collectors use "quarto" to describe old books produced in the quarto format — meaning, the original printing sheet was folded twice to create four leaves. When a bibliographer says a book is "a quarto," they are making a very specific, technical statement about how that book was manufactured.

2. As a general size description: In modern publishing, "quarto" (sometimes written as "4to" in shorthand) is occasionally used to loosely describe a book or paper size that falls in the quarto range — roughly 9 to 12 inches tall. This usage is less strict and doesn't necessarily imply the traditional folding process; it is more of a shorthand for "a page about that size."

To keep things perfectly clear:

  • A quarto is not just any large-ish book. The word has a specific technical meaning tied to the folding of a printing sheet.
  • A quarto is not defined by an exact, fixed set of inch measurements. The size varied throughout history depending on the printer and the original sheet used.
  • A quarto is not the same as a folio (which is bigger, folded only once) or an octavo (which is smaller, folded three times).

If you had to reduce "quarto" to its clearest possible form: a quarto is a book or document where the original sheet of paper was folded twice, producing four leaves and eight pages, with each page being one-quarter the size of the original sheet.

Everything else — the historical significance, the Shakespeare connection, the approximate measurements — is context built on top of that single, simple idea.
13135: A quasar is an extraordinarily powerful, extremely distant celestial object — the brilliantly glowing core of a very young galaxy, powered by a colossal black hole devouring enormous amounts of matter.
Breaking that down, piece by piece

The black hole at the heart

Every large galaxy — including our own Milky Way — has a supermassive black hole sitting at its very center. These are not ordinary black holes. They can be millions or even billions of times heavier than our Sun. Normally, a black hole just sits there quietly. But sometimes, vast clouds of gas, dust, and shredded stars fall toward it in huge quantities. That's when things get dramatic.

The engine: why quasars glow so intensely

You might expect that matter falling into a black hole simply disappears. But before it crosses the point of no return, something remarkable happens. All that infalling material gets squeezed into a rapidly spinning, flattened disk called an accretion disk — think of water swirling around a drain, but at cosmic scale. As the material spins and spirals inward, particles constantly crash into each other, creating enormous friction. This friction heats the disk to temperatures of millions of degrees. At those temperatures, the disk doesn't just glow — it blazes, releasing energy across the entire electromagnetic spectrum: visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays, and sometimes powerful jets of particles shooting out from both poles like cosmic flamethrowers.

This process — matter being compressed and heated before being consumed — is one of the most efficient energy-conversion mechanisms in the known universe, far more efficient than nuclear fusion (the process that powers stars). A quasar converts roughly 10% of its infalling matter directly into energy. By comparison, the Sun converts less than 1% in nuclear fusion.

Just how bright are they?

The numbers are almost impossible to grasp. A single quasar can outshine an entire galaxy of hundreds of billions of stars — sometimes by a factor of 100 or even 1,000. The most luminous quasars pour out energy equivalent to tens of trillions of Suns, all from a region smaller than our solar system. The core of a galaxy — a tiny speck compared to the galaxy itself — can be so blindingly bright that it completely drowns out all the stars around it.

This is why quasars were originally thought to be strange, isolated "star-like" objects when first observed. They looked like single points of light, yet they were far too bright and energetic to be any known type of star.
Distance: quasars are windows into the ancient universe

Here's something crucial: quasars are not scattered all around the universe. The vast majority of them are incredibly far away — billions of light-years from Earth. Because light takes time to travel, when we observe something billions of light-years away, we're seeing it as it was billions of years ago. In other words, we're looking back in time.

This means quasars are objects from the early universe — from an era roughly 1 to 3 billion years after the Big Bang, when the universe was young, galaxies were actively forming, and supermassive black holes had abundant fuel to consume. As the universe aged, galaxies gradually "used up" the raw material surrounding their central black holes. The feeding slowed down, the accretion disks faded, and quasars went quiet. That's why we don't see many quasars nearby: the conditions that created them no longer widely exist in the modern universe.

Our own Milky Way has a supermassive black hole at its center (called Sagittarius A*), and it was probably a quasar billions of years ago. Today it's essentially dormant — it has run out of nearby material to consume in large quantities.

In the late 1950s and early 1960s, astronomers mapping the sky with radio telescopes detected powerful sources of radio waves that had no obvious visible counterpart. When optical telescopes were turned to the same spots, they found what appeared to be faint stars. But stars don't emit that kind of radio energy. These objects were puzzling.

The key breakthrough came in 1963 when astronomer Maarten Schmidt studied one of these objects — known as 3C 273 — and measured its redshift. Redshift is the stretching of light toward the red end of the spectrum that happens when an object is moving away from you very rapidly. Schmidt found that 3C 273 was moving away at enormous speed, meaning it was extraordinarily far away — about 2.4 billion light-years. For something that far away to appear visible at all, it had to be putting out an almost unimaginable amount of energy. This was the realization that changed astronomy: these weren't strange stars at all — they were incredibly distant, incredibly powerful objects of an entirely new class. The name quasi-stellar object was coined, quickly shortened to quasar.
What quasars look like from Earth

Even the closest known quasar (3C 273) is about 2.4 billion light-years away. At those distances, even with their extraordinary brightness, quasars appear as tiny, faint pinpoints of light to the naked eye — most are far too faint to see without telescopes. Through an optical telescope, most quasars look like very faint stars. Only by studying their light in detail — measuring its spectrum and redshift — can astronomers confirm what they're really looking at. Modern instruments can detect quasars that are over 13 billion light-years away, meaning we're seeing them as they existed when the universe was less than a billion years old.

Quasars belong to a broader family of objects astronomers call Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) — a general term for any galaxy whose central black hole is actively and powerfully consuming matter. The different names within this family — Seyfert galaxies, blazars, radio galaxies, quasars — largely depend on how luminous the AGN is and the angle from which we're viewing it.

  • A blazar is essentially a quasar whose jet of particles happens to be aimed almost directly at Earth, making it appear even more intense and variable.
  • A Seyfert galaxy is like a quieter, less luminous version of a quasar — still active, but not nearly as extreme.
  • A radio-loud quasar shoots powerful jets detectable in radio waves; a radio-quiet quasar (the majority) does not, but still blazes in visible light and X-rays.

All of them share the same fundamental engine: a supermassive black hole with an accretion disk.

Beyond being fascinating objects in their own right, quasars are enormously useful tools for understanding the universe.

As cosmic backdrops, quasars are so bright and so far away that their light passes through billions of light-years of intergalactic space before reaching us. Along the way, that light gets subtly absorbed by hydrogen gas clouds and other matter it passes through. By analyzing exactly which wavelengths of light are absorbed, astronomers can map the large-scale structure of matter in the universe across cosmic time — almost like reading the fingerprints of everything the light traveled through.

As timekeepers, because quasars were abundant in the early universe and rare today, they reveal how dramatically the universe has evolved. Studying quasars at different distances (and therefore different eras) shows us how galaxies and their central black holes grew together. This has led to one of the surprising findings of modern astronomy: the mass of a galaxy's central black hole is closely related to the size of the galaxy itself, suggesting that quasars and their host galaxies shaped each other's growth.

As probes of the very early universe, the most distant quasars tell us about a time so early that the universe hadn't yet fully "cleared up" after the Big Bang. Studying this era — called the Epoch of Reionization — is one of the frontiers of modern cosmology.

A quasar is the violently luminous core of a young, distant galaxy, where a supermassive black hole is actively consuming vast amounts of matter. As that matter spirals in, it heats to millions of degrees and releases more energy than entire galaxies of stars — making quasars the brightest sustained objects in the universe. Because they're so far away, we see them as relics of the early cosmos. They are simultaneously extreme physical phenomena, cosmic time capsules, and some of the most powerful tools astronomers have for understanding how the universe came to be the way it is today.
13136: "Quash" means to put a complete and forceful end to something — so thoroughly that it cannot come back. It's not about slowing something down or weakening it. It's about eliminating it entirely, often in a single decisive act.

When you quash something, you crush it, stamp it out, or shut it down completely. The thing being quashed is usually something that has started to grow, spread, or cause trouble — like a rebellion, a rumor, or even a feeling. And the person doing the quashing is usually someone in a position of power or authority.

Examples in real life:

"The army was sent in to quash the uprising." — The rebellion was crushed completely, not just slowed down.

"The company released a statement to quash rumors about its bankruptcy." — They put a firm, definitive end to those rumors.

"She struggled to quash her feelings of jealousy." — She was trying to suppress those feelings so they wouldn't surface.

"The teacher quashed any attempt at cheating immediately." — She shut it down the moment it appeared.
The Single Most Important Nuance: Totality

This is what makes "quash" different from words like "reduce" or "discourage." When you quash something, you don't merely push it back — you finish it off completely, or at least intend to.

Compare these two sentences:

"The government tried to reduce the protests." — A mild, partial effort.

"The government quashed the protests." — A forceful, complete crackdown.

The second sentence is much stronger. "Quash" implies that whatever was rising up has been definitively put down.

In legal contexts, "quash" has a precise technical meaning: a court or judge officially declares something legally invalid — cancelling it as if it never had legal standing. This is an authoritative ruling, not just an opinion.

Common things that get quashed in law include convictions, warrants, subpoenas (official demands to appear in court or hand over evidence), indictments, and court orders.

Examples:

"The appeals court quashed his conviction." — His conviction was declared legally void. He was no longer officially convicted.

"The judge quashed the subpoena." — The demand for someone to produce documents or testify was officially cancelled.

"The lawyers successfully quashed the arrest warrant." — The warrant was declared legally invalid and could no longer be acted upon.

Notice how the legal meaning still connects to the core idea — something is being completely and decisively ended. The key difference is that in law, it happens through a formal, official ruling by someone with judicial authority.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Quashed?

Understanding the company "quash" keeps will help you use and recognize it naturally. Here are the most common categories:

Unrest and resistance: a rebellion, a revolt, an uprising, opposition, dissent, a protest, a coup attempt.

Rumors and speculation: quash rumors, quash speculation, quash reports that something is happening.

Emotions, hopes, and ideas: quash feelings of doubt, quash someone's enthusiasm, quash hopes, quash excitement, quash a theory.

Legal matters: quash a conviction, a warrant, a subpoena, an indictment, an appeal, a court order.

Suppress is the closest word in meaning. The difference is subtle: "suppress" often implies an ongoing effort to hold something down (you suppress a cough, you suppress feelings over time), while "quash" tends to feel like one decisive, final act (you quash a rebellion in a single military response). That said, they overlap heavily and are sometimes interchangeable.

Crush is more physically violent and aggressive in tone. "Quash" is just as firm, but it fits more naturally in official, abstract, and legal contexts — you'd see it in a newspaper more easily than in a battle scene.

Squash sounds almost identical and shares the same root. In informal, everyday speech, people sometimes use "squash" and "quash" interchangeably. However, in formal writing and especially in legal language, "quash" is always the correct choice. Think of "quash" as the more serious, grown-up version.

Nullify and void overlap with the legal meaning of "quash," but they feel more passive and technical — they describe a state or outcome. "Quash" emphasizes the active, authoritative act of someone making it happen.

"Quash" sits in the formal-to-neutral range. You'll encounter it most in news articles, legal documents, and official statements. In casual spoken conversation, people tend to say things like "shut it down," "stamp it out," or "kill it" instead. But "quash" is not so stiff that it sounds out of place in normal writing or moderately formal speech. It's a reliable, precise word to reach for when you want to convey that something was ended completely and with authority.
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All
To quash something = to put a total, forceful, and authoritative end to it — whether that's a rebellion, a rumor, a feeling, or a legal order.
13137:
"Quasi" means almost, but not quite — or more precisely: resembling something, but not truly being that thing in the full, genuine, or official sense.

When you place "quasi" before a noun, you are saying: "This thing shares features with [that noun], looks or acts like [that noun], but it does not completely qualify as [that noun]." It signals a middle ground — the thing is too similar to ignore the comparison, yet too different to use the word directly.

Think of "quasi" as a word that draws a careful line between resemblance and identity.
The Three Shades of Its Meaning

"Quasi" carries slightly different flavors depending on context, but they all orbit the same core idea:

1. Almost / Partially
The thing has many qualities of X, but not all of them. Something is incomplete — it falls just short.

A "quasi-democracy" has some democratic features, like elections or a parliament, but lacks others, like a truly free press or fair voting. It is not fully a democracy, but it is not entirely without democratic qualities either. It lives somewhere in between.

2. Seeming / Apparent (but not genuinely real)
The thing looks like X on the surface, but does not hold up under closer examination.

A "quasi-scientific" claim uses the appearance of science — charts, technical-sounding words, references to data — but does not follow proper scientific methods or standards. It wears the costume of science without earning the title.

3. Functioning like X, but not officially X
The thing operates the way X does — it plays the same role, has similar powers — but lacks the official status or full authority of X.

A "quasi-judicial" body makes decisions and rulings in the manner of a court, but it is not a court of law in the official, legal sense.

Picture a "quasi-friend." This is someone you occasionally spend time with, exchange small favors with, and might contact when you need help. But you would not call them a true friend — there is no deep trust, no long shared history, no real emotional bond.

They occupy the space between a stranger and a genuine friend.

That in-between quality — close enough to compare, yet different enough to not fully qualify — is the beating heart of "quasi."

This is where many learners go wrong, so pay attention:

It does not mean fake or dishonest. A quasi-democracy is a real political system that actually exists. "Quasi" is not accusing it of being a lie — only of being incomplete.

It is not a negative judgment by itself. "Quasi" is a neutral, precise word. It does not automatically mean something is bad, inferior, or suspicious. It simply means limited or partial.

It does not mean the opposite. A "quasi-scientific" idea is not anti-science — it is science-adjacent. It is closer to science than to art, but it does not fully reach the bar of science.

Seeing it in multiple real-world areas will cement your understanding:

Legal: A "quasi-contract" is an obligation that courts treat like a contract and enforce similarly, even though the two parties never actually agreed to a formal contract. The law uses the logic and rules of contracts without there being a true contract.

Political: A "quasi-government agency" operates like a government body — it may receive public funding, serve public interests, follow government-like rules — but it is not technically a part of the government itself.

Social: A "quasi-celebrity" is someone who enjoys a degree of fame within a limited circle, perhaps a popular local musician or a niche internet creator, but has not reached the level of a true celebrity with widespread recognition.

Academic research: A "quasi-experimental study" is designed to resemble a proper scientific experiment, but it is missing one critical ingredient — for example, it does not randomly assign participants to groups. This one gap disqualifies it from being called a true experiment, even though everything else about it looks like one.

When a writer or speaker uses "quasi," there is almost always an undertone of careful, honest precision. They are essentially saying:

"I am not comfortable calling this thing [X] outright, because it does not fully earn that label — but it resembles [X] closely enough that comparing it to [X] is the clearest way to describe it to you."

It is a word used by someone who is paying attention to detail, unwilling to exaggerate, but also unwilling to ignore a clear resemblance. It holds two truths at once: yes, it looks like this and no, it is not quite this.
One Final Way to Cement It

Whenever you see "quasi-" before a word, ask yourself two questions:

  1. What is the full, genuine version of this thing?
  2. What is this version missing — or only partly having — that prevents it from being the real thing?

The answer to question 2 is exactly the gap that "quasi" is pointing to. Master that gap, and you have mastered the word.
13138:
"Quaternary" is an adjective that revolves entirely around one idea: the number four. Something described as quaternary is either made up of four parts, belongs to a fourth stage in a sequence, or is organized around a group of four elements.

Think of it this way: you already know the family this word belongs to — primary (first), secondary (second), tertiary (third), and then quaternary (fourth). Each step adds one more. Quaternary is simply what comes after tertiary.

That's the backbone of the word. Everything else below is just this same idea applied in different fields.

In its broadest sense, you can call anything "quaternary" if it has four components or occupies a fourth position in a ranking or order. A quaternary group is a group of four. A quaternary stage is a fourth stage. This general usage is rare in casual conversation but does appear in scientific, academic, and technical writing.

Chemistry is one of the most common places where you'll encounter this word, and it appears in a few distinct ways.

A quaternary carbon atom is a carbon atom that is bonded to exactly four other carbon atoms — and no hydrogen atoms at all. Since carbon can form exactly four bonds, a quaternary carbon has used all four of those bonds on carbon neighbours alone. This is important in chemistry because it affects how a molecule behaves and reacts.

A quaternary ammonium compound is a molecule where a nitrogen atom is bonded to four organic groups (carbon-based groups) instead of the usual fewer. These compounds are widely used in disinfectants, fabric softeners, and preservatives.

More generally, a quaternary compound or quaternary mixture in chemistry simply means one that contains four distinct chemical elements or components.

Proteins, the workhorses of your body, are built in layers of increasing complexity. Scientists describe four levels of protein structure, and "quaternary" names the fourth and most complex level.

A protein's quaternary structure refers to the way multiple separate protein chains (called subunits) come together and arrange themselves into a single, fully functioning unit. Not all proteins have a quaternary structure — only those built from two or more chains do. A famous example is haemoglobin, the protein in your red blood cells that carries oxygen. It is made of four separate protein chains that lock together into one working molecule. That assembly of four chains is its quaternary structure.

In short: if a protein is a machine, the quaternary structure is the final assembled machine made up of multiple parts.

This is arguably the most widely known use of the word, especially in Earth sciences.

The Quaternary is the name of the current geological period — the stretch of Earth's history we are living in right now. It began approximately 2.58 million years ago and continues to the present day. The name came from early geologists who divided Earth's rock history into four broad stages; this was the fourth and most recent one.

The Quaternary Period is divided into two smaller units called epochs:

The Pleistocene epoch spans from 2.58 million years ago to about 11,700 years ago. This was the age of great ice ages, when massive glaciers repeatedly advanced and retreated across continents. It was also the age of megafauna — woolly mammoths, sabre-toothed cats, giant ground sloths — and the period during which early humans evolved and spread across the Earth.

The Holocene epoch covers the last 11,700 years to the present. As the last ice age ended and the climate warmed, the Holocene became the era in which human civilization took root — farming, cities, writing, and everything that followed.

Some scientists today also discuss an Anthropocene epoch as a proposed new subdivision, marking the period in which human activity has become the dominant force shaping the planet's geology and environment, though this is still debated in the scientific community.

A quaternary numeral system (also called base-4) is a way of counting and writing numbers using only four digits: 0, 1, 2, and 3. Just as our familiar decimal system is base-10 (using digits 0–9) and binary is base-2 (using only 0 and 1), the quaternary system builds all numbers from combinations of just those four digits. It is used in certain areas of computing and mathematics.

Medicine organizes care into levels based on how specialized and complex the treatment is.

Primary care is your first point of contact — a general practitioner or family doctor. Secondary care is a referral to a specialist or a general hospital. Tertiary care involves highly specialized hospitals that handle complex conditions. Quaternary care is the fourth and most advanced level — it refers to experimental, cutting-edge, or extraordinarily rare treatments that only a handful of research hospitals in the world can provide. Think of clinical trials, pioneering surgeries, or treatment for extremely rare diseases.

Some economists extend the classic three-sector model of an economy (primary: farming and resource extraction; secondary: manufacturing; tertiary: services) by adding a quaternary sector. This fourth sector covers knowledge-based activities — information technology, research and development, education, financial planning, and media. The idea is that in modern economies, the creation, management, and distribution of knowledge and information deserves its own category beyond general services.
The One Thread That Ties It All Together

No matter where you encounter "quaternary" — in a chemistry textbook, a geology lecture, a biology class, a hospital, or an economics paper — it always leads back to the same root idea: four. It is either something in a fourth position, something composed of four parts, or something belonging to a fourth and often most advanced stage in a progression.

Once you have that anchor in your mind, the word will never confuse you again regardless of the context it appears in.
13139:
A quatrain is a set of four lines in a poem. That's the heart of it. The word itself simply means "a unit of four poetic lines."

These four lines are held together — they feel like they belong as a group, usually because of how they rhyme or how their meaning fits together.

This is an important distinction that many learners miss:

1. A quatrain can be an entire, complete poem — just four lines, start to finish. The whole poem is the quatrain.

2. A quatrain can be one stanza (a "block" of lines) inside a longer poem. Just like a paragraph is one chunk of a longer essay, a quatrain is one four-line chunk of a longer poem. A poem can have two quatrains, five quatrains, ten — as many as the poet needs.

Think of stanzas like chapters in a book. A quatrain is simply a "chapter" that always has exactly four lines.

Quatrains usually (though not always) follow a rhyme scheme — a pattern that describes which lines rhyme with which. Poets use letters to map these patterns, where the same letter means the lines rhyme with each other.

Here are the four most common rhyme schemes in quatrains:

ABAB — Alternating Rhyme (the most common of all)
Lines 1 and 3 rhyme with each other. Lines 2 and 4 rhyme with each other.

The sun descends beyond the hill, (A)
And paints the sky in red and gold, (B)
The evening air grows calm and still, (A)
And ancient tales are gently told. (B)

Notice: hill and still rhyme (A), and gold and told rhyme (B). The rhymes alternate like a zigzag.

AABB — Paired Rhyme (or "Couplet" rhyme)
Lines 1 and 2 rhyme. Lines 3 and 4 rhyme. The rhymes come in pairs.

The river flows without a care, (A)
Its song drifts lightly through the air, (A)
The fish dart silver, swift, and bright, (B)
Like scattered sparks of dancing light. (B)

ABBA — Enclosed Rhyme (or "Envelope" rhyme)
Lines 1 and 4 rhyme. Lines 2 and 3 rhyme. The outer lines "wrap around" the inner ones like an envelope.

The moonlight falls upon the lake, (A)
And fills the night with silver glow, (B)
The reeds sway gently, soft and slow, (B)
As ripples spread across its wake. (A)

Notice how lake and wake are on the outside, wrapping around glow and slow on the inside.

ABCB — Ballad Rhyme
Only lines 2 and 4 rhyme. Lines 1 and 3 don't rhyme with anything. This is the looser, more casual-sounding scheme, common in folk songs, hymns, and ballads.

A soldier walked the dusty road, (A — doesn't rhyme)
His boots worn down to leather, (B)
He thought of home and fields of wheat, (C — doesn't rhyme)
And skies of storm and weather. (B)

Can a quatrain have no rhyme at all?
Yes. A quatrain can be written in free verse, meaning the lines don't rhyme at all. What makes it a quatrain is purely the count — four lines grouped together. The rhyme scheme is a feature, not a requirement.

Quatrains are one of the oldest and most widely used forms in all of poetry. They appear everywhere:

Shakespeare's Sonnets — A Shakespearean sonnet has 14 lines arranged as three quatrains followed by a final two-line rhyming pair (called a couplet). The three quatrains each develop part of an idea, and the couplet wraps it up. So the quatrain was actually a building block of one of history's most celebrated poetry forms.

The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam — This is a famous Persian poem (later translated into English by Edward FitzGerald) made up entirely of individual quatrains. Each four-line unit tells its own small thought or idea. The word ruba'i in Persian actually means "quatrain," which tells you how central this form was to that tradition.

Hymns and songs — A huge number of hymns, folk songs, and even modern song lyrics are naturally written in quatrains, usually with ABCB or ABAB rhyme schemes. When you sing a hymn in church or a classic folk song, you are very likely singing quatrain after quatrain.

Emily Dickinson — The American poet Emily Dickinson wrote almost all of her poetry in quatrains, nearly always using the ABCB (ballad) rhyme scheme. Her poems are simple-looking on the surface but carry enormous emotional depth — all packed into these tight four-line units.
Why Four Lines? Why Is This Form So Popular?

The quatrain is popular for the same reason that things like the three-act structure in storytelling are popular — the human mind naturally finds a certain number of parts satisfying.

Four lines give a poet just enough space to:

  • Set up an idea (lines 1–2)
  • Turn or develop it (line 3)
  • Land or resolve it (line 4)

It's compact but not cramped. It's complete but not rambling. This makes it versatile — it works for a quick observation, a love poem, a moment of grief, a joke, or a grand philosophical idea.

Ask yourself two questions when reading a poem:

  1. Are these lines grouped into visible blocks with a gap (white space) between them?
  2. Does each block have exactly four lines?

If yes to both — those blocks are quatrains.

If the entire poem has only four lines and no blocks — the whole poem is itself one quatrain.

ConceptWhat it means

A quatrain is a four-line unit of poetry. It can be a complete poem on its own, or one stanza within a longer poem. It usually follows a rhyme scheme — most commonly ABAB, AABB, ABBA, or ABCB — but it doesn't have to rhyme at all. It is one of the most fundamental and widely used building blocks in all of world poetry, found in everything from Shakespeare's sonnets to hymns to ancient Persian verse.

If you can count to four and spot a group of lines — you can spot a quatrain.
